entities.name: Dao De Jing (Tao Te Ching)
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The foundational text of philosophical Daoism, traditionally attributed to Laozi (the "Old Master"), a semi-legendary contemporary or near-contemporary of Confucius, though modern scholarship dates it to the 4th–3rd century BCE. In only 81 brief chapters (approximately 5,000 Chinese characters), the Dao De Jing articulates a profound philosophy of the Dao (the Way — the ineffable, all-pervading source and principle of reality), De (virtue/power as manifestation of Dao), wu wei (non-action, effortless action — letting things take their natural course), and the paradoxical wisdom of softness over hardness, emptiness over fullness, yielding over force.

Its opening line — "The Dao that can be spoken is not the eternal Dao" (Dao ke dao, fei chang Dao) — is among the most famous sentences in world philosophy. With over 250 translations, the Dao De Jing is the most translated Chinese text and one of the most translated works in any language, second only to the Bible.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Dao De Jing's influence can be seen in the development of East Asian thought and culture, shaping the philosophies of Confucianism and Buddhism. Its concepts of wu wei and the paradox of softness over hardness have inspired countless thinkers and artists throughout history.
